# Datatypes

Value types rather than Instances. **Constructors and constants are reached
through the namespace and are camelCase** (`CFrame.new`, `CFrame.identity`);
**members reached through a value are PascalCase** (`v.Magnitude`,
`cf:Inverse()`). That split is ADR 0034 and it is the whole naming rule.

## AnimationTrack

One clip playing on one `AnimationPlayer`, returned by `LoadAnimation` (§2.2). A handle rather than an Instance, like `Tween`: nothing parents a track and nothing finds one in the tree.

It is also the one datatype here that is not immutable, and the reason is what a handle IS: `track.Looped = true` names the one track every holder of that handle can see, where `cf.Position = v` would write to a copy the caller is about to drop.

**Its clock is the SimClock's.** `Speed` scales it, sampling happens at `PreAnimation`, and nothing here reads a wall clock -- so a clip is at the same position on the same tick in a replay as it was live.

## AnimationTrack — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Ended` | `Signal<>` | — | read-only | Fires on the tick a track reaches the end of a clip that is not `Looped`. A PROPERTY here rather than an event because a track is not a class and only classes declare events; the signal it holds behaves like any other.<br><br>A `Stop` does not fire it: it is a past-tense fact about reaching the end, and code that chains the next animation on it must not be fooled by one that was interrupted. |
| `Length` | `number` | — | read-only | The clip's duration in seconds, or zero for a track whose clip was not found. |
| `Looped` | `boolean` | — | read/write | Whether reaching the end wraps to the start instead of stopping. A looped track never fires `Ended`, because it never does. Wrapping keeps the fraction of a tick it overshot by, so a loop does not drift against everything else in the scene. |
| `Playing` | `boolean` | — | read-only | Whether the clock is advancing. False for a track that reached the end of a clip that is not `Looped` -- which still HOLDS its last frame until it is stopped or replayed, because `Ended` is deferred and a character that returned to its rest pose for the one tick before the handler ran would be a visible pop. |
| `Speed` | `number` | — | read/write | How fast the clip's clock runs. 2 is twice the speed and half the duration; 0 holds the pose where it is, which is the honest way to freeze a frame. |
| `TimePosition` | `number` | — | read-only | Where the clip's clock is, in seconds. Read-only in v1: seeking a blended pose is a different feature from playing one, and a writable seek that ignored the blend would be the wrong half of it. |
| `Weight` | `number` | — | read/write | How much this track contributes when several drive one skeleton. Assigning it is immediate -- the faded form is `Play`'s and `Stop`'s argument, and a property that took a fade time would not be a property.<br><br>Blending is a weighted average PER JOINT and per component, so a joint no clip drives keeps its rest transform rather than being dragged towards the origin by tracks that say nothing about it. |

## AnimationTrack — methods

### `Play(fadeTime: number?)`

Starts the clip from the BEGINNING, every time -- the opposite of `Tween:Play`, and deliberately: a jump animation triggered twice should play twice.

`fadeTime` fades the weight in from zero over that many seconds, which is what makes a walk blend into an idle rather than snapping. It fades in to this track's own `Weight`, which is why one argument is enough.

### `Stop(fadeTime: number?)`

Ends the track. `fadeTime` fades its weight out over that many seconds and stops it when it reaches zero; without one it stops on the spot. `Ended` does not fire either way.

## CFrame

A rigid transform: an orthonormal rotation basis plus a translation. The translation is **f64** and is the world-precision source of truth the whole engine is built around (ADR 0014) -- `Position` is its f32 rounding, so gameplay math past a few kilometres from the origin must stay in CFrame rather than round-tripping through a vector. The world is right-handed, Y-up, -Z forward, matching glTF, and every sign in this type follows from that. Operators: `CFrame * CFrame` composes, `CFrame * vector` transforms a **point** (the translation is applied), and `==` is exact and component-wise -- an identity test, never a tolerance.

## CFrame — constants

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `identity` | `CFrame` | — | read-only | The identity transform: no rotation, at the origin. `cf * CFrame.identity == cf`. |

## CFrame — constructors

### `fromAxisAngle(axis: vector, angle: number): CFrame`

A rotation of `angle` radians about `axis` by the right-hand rule, at the origin. The axis is normalized on the way in, so its length carries no meaning.

### `fromEuler(rx: number, ry: number, rz: number, order: Enum.RotationOrder? = Enum.RotationOrder.YXZ): CFrame`

The ONE euler constructor -- there is no `fromEulerAnglesXYZ`/`YXZ` family, because the order belongs in an argument and not in a name. Angles are radians, applied as **intrinsic** rotations in `order` (each about the axes the previous one produced) and signed by the right-hand rule about each axis.

### `fromMatrix(position: vector, right: vector, up: vector, back: vector): CFrame`

A frame built from an explicit basis. The third axis is **back**, not forward, so `LookVector == -back`. Axes that are neither unit length nor mutually perpendicular are stored as given: a constructor that silently repaired its input would hide the bug that produced it. `Orthonormalize` is the explicit repair.

### `fromQuaternion(position: vector, qx: number, qy: number, qz: number, qw: number): CFrame`

A frame at `position` rotated by the quaternion `(qx, qy, qz, qw)` -- w last, matching `ToQuaternion`'s tail, which is the half of the convention people get wrong. The quaternion is normalized on the way in.

### `lookAt(position: vector, target: vector, up: vector? = Vector3.new(0, 1, 0)): CFrame`

A frame at `position` whose `LookVector` points at `target`, with `up` biasing the roll and defaulting to `(0, 1, 0)`. Where the direction is degenerate or `up` is parallel to it the result is the identity rotation at `position`, not a frame full of NaN: a camera pointed at itself should stop moving, not poison every value it touches.

### `new(position: vector): CFrame`

A frame with the identity rotation at `position`. The overload exists so a vector does not have to be unpacked to be placed, but it enters through f32 -- construct from numbers where the extra precision matters.

### `new(x: number? = 0, y: number? = 0, z: number? = 0): CFrame`

A frame with the identity rotation at the given position; a missing component is 0, so `CFrame.new()` is the identity. The components are taken as f64 and stored as f64.

## CFrame — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `LookVector` | `vector` | — | read-only | The basis's **-Z** column -- forward is -Z in a right-handed Y-up world, which is why `RightVector:Cross(UpVector) == -LookVector` rather than `LookVector`. |
| `Position` | `vector` | — | read-only | The translation, rounded from f64 to f32 at every magnitude -- reading it is lossy far from the origin and reading it twice is not (the rounding is a function, not a drift). The f64 value never leaves the CFrame, which is what makes composing transforms exact where composing positions is not. |
| `RightVector` | `vector` | — | read-only | The basis's +X column. |
| `Rotation` | `CFrame` | — | read-only | The same rotation basis with a zero translation, so a pure translation's `Rotation` is the identity. This is what the `VectorTo*Space` pair is defined in terms of. |
| `UpVector` | `vector` | — | read-only | The basis's +Y column. |

## CFrame — methods

### `Inverse(): CFrame`

The transform that undoes this one: `cf * cf:Inverse() == CFrame.identity` up to floating-point rounding.

### `Lerp(goal: CFrame, alpha: number): CFrame`

Interpolates the translation linearly and **slerps** the rotation, so the halfway frame sits at an equal angle from each end rather than cutting the corner. `alpha` is not clamped and values outside [0, 1] extrapolate.

### `Orthonormalize(): CFrame`

Repairs a drifted or hand-built basis, preserving the translation and treating `LookVector` as authoritative: the look direction is normalized, `UpVector` is made perpendicular to it and normalized, and `RightVector` is whatever their cross product requires. This is the explicit counterpart to `fromMatrix` storing what it is given.

### `PointToObjectSpace(point: vector): vector`

Moves a world-space **position** into this frame, translation included. Defined as `self:Inverse() * point`.

### `PointToWorldSpace(point: vector): vector`

Moves a **position** out of this frame into world space, translation included. Defined as `self * point`.

### `ToAxisAngle(): (vector, number)`

Decomposes the rotation into `(axis, angle)` with a unit axis and the angle in radians; the inverse of `fromAxisAngle`.

### `ToEuler(order: Enum.RotationOrder? = Enum.RotationOrder.YXZ): (number, number, number)`

Decomposes the rotation into `(rx, ry, rz)` radians in `fromEuler`'s parameter order, and is its inverse for the same `order`. Euler angles are not unique, so a round trip returns an equivalent rotation rather than necessarily the same three numbers.

### `ToObjectSpace(cf: CFrame): CFrame`

Expresses the world-space frame `cf` relative to this one. Defined as `self:Inverse() * cf`.

### `ToQuaternion(): (number, number, number, number)`

Decomposes the rotation into `(qx, qy, qz, qw)` -- w last, matching `fromQuaternion`'s tail, whose inverse this is.

### `ToWorldSpace(cf: CFrame): CFrame`

Reads `cf` as being expressed relative to this frame and returns it in world space. Defined as `self * cf`.

### `VectorToObjectSpace(direction: vector): vector`

Moves a world-space **direction** into this frame, rotation only. Defined as `self.Rotation:Inverse() * direction`.

### `VectorToWorldSpace(direction: vector): vector`

Moves a **direction** out of this frame into world space, rotation only. Defined as `self.Rotation * direction`. A surface normal run through `PointToWorldSpace` instead comes out wrong by exactly the frame's position.

## CFrame — operators

| Operator | Signature | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `__mul` | `(other: CFrame): CFrame` | Composes two transforms: `a * b` reads as "first `b`, then `a`", the column-vector convention every matrix in the engine follows. |
| `__mul` | `(point: vector): vector` | Transforms a **point** -- the translation is applied. `VectorToWorldSpace` is the direction form, and a surface normal put through this one comes out wrong by exactly the frame's position. |
| `__eq` | `(other: CFrame): boolean` | Exact and component-wise: an identity test, never a tolerance. Two frames built by different routes to the same place are equal only if every stored number matches. |

## Color3

An RGB colour in three f32 channels, nominally 0-1 and deliberately **not clamped**: values outside the range are legal and meaningful for HDR emissives and tint multipliers over 1, so clamping belongs to the consumer that actually has a range to respect. No BrickColor. `==` is exact and component-wise.

## Color3 — constructors

### `fromHSV(h: number, s: number, v: number): Color3`

A colour from hue, saturation and value -- **all three** 0-1, hue included, so `fromHSV(1/3, 1, 1)` is green and not a hue of one third of a degree.

### `fromHex(hex: string): Color3`

A colour from a hex string, accepting `#rrggbb`, `rrggbb`, `#rgb` and `rgb` case-insensitively, so the round trip with `ToHex` is defined in both directions and neither call has to guess what the other meant. Anything else raises `script.err.color_hex_invalid` rather than returning a silently wrong colour.

### `fromRGB(r: number, g: number, b: number): Color3`

A colour from three 0-255 channels, which is the range colour pickers and design tools speak in. The channels are divided by 255 and stored, not rounded to a byte.

### `new(r: number? = 0, g: number? = 0, b: number? = 0): Color3`

A colour from three 0-1 channels, each defaulting to 0, so `Color3.new()` is black. Out-of-range values are kept as given.

## Color3 — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `B` | `number` | — | read-only | The blue channel, nominally 0-1 and not clamped. |
| `G` | `number` | — | read-only | The green channel, nominally 0-1 and not clamped. |
| `R` | `number` | — | read-only | The red channel, nominally 0-1 and not clamped. `c.r` raises `script.err.unknown_member`: there is one spelling. |

## Color3 — methods

### `Lerp(goal: Color3, alpha: number): Color3`

Channel-wise linear interpolation toward `goal` in RGB, which is the cheap blend and not the perceptually even one. `alpha` is not clamped.

### `ToHSV(): (number, number, number)`

Decomposes the colour into `(h, s, v)`, all three 0-1; the inverse of `fromHSV`. Hue is undefined for a grey and reported as 0.

### `ToHex(): string`

Six lowercase hex digits with no leading `#` (`"ff8800"`). The channels are clamped into 0-255 on the way out because eight bits cannot represent anything else -- this is the one place a Color3 is narrowed, and it is why the round trip through `fromHex` does not preserve an HDR value.

## Color3 — operators

| Operator | Signature | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `__eq` | `(other: Color3): boolean` | Exact and component-wise. Channels are not clamped, so two colours that would render identically after clamping are still unequal if their stored values differ. |

## Connection

The handle a `Signal:Connect` or `:Once` returns -- never `RBXScriptConnection` (divergence #4). Its only job is to end the connection it represents; it is not constructible on its own.

## Connection — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Connected` | `boolean` | — | read-only | Whether the connection is still live. False after `Disconnect`, after the owning signal is destroyed, and after a `:Once` handler has run. No `Is` prefix: boolean properties do not carry one, boolean methods do (§9). |

## Connection — methods

### `Disconnect()`

Ends the connection. **Idempotent**: a second call is a no-op and `Connected` stays false, so cleanup code never has to guard it. A fire already on the queue captured its connection list before this call, so it may still have invoked the handler.

## InputObject

One raw input, as `InputService.InputBegan`, `InputChanged` and `InputEnded` carry it (§2.4, ADR 0041). A read-only SNAPSHOT and not a live object: it describes what happened on one tick, and a handler that stashes one is holding a fact rather than a handle.

**These events come from the Input Action System''s own dispatch, not from the operating system.** Same source, same tick, after the UI has consumed what it consumed -- and in a replay they come from the recorded stream, so a recorded run reproduces every input a game reads.

## InputObject — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Delta` | `vector` | — | read-only | How much it moved since the last tick, in the same units as `Position`. `z` is the wheel movement, which is where a `MouseWheel` event puts its one number. Zero for anything that is not motion. |
| `KeyCode` | `Enum.KeyCode` | — | read-only | Which key, button or axis. `Unknown` for pointer motion and the wheel, which are not keys -- and `Unknown` is a real item rather than nil precisely so this property never has to be checked before it is compared. |
| `Position` | `vector` | — | read-only | Where the pointer is, in window pixels with the origin at the top left, with `z` carrying the accumulated wheel. For a gamepad axis it is the deflection instead: `x` and `y` for a stick, `x` alone for a trigger.<br><br>A three-wide vector rather than a `Vector2` because `vector` is this engine''s native primitive (ADR 0013) -- it costs no userdata and no allocation, which matters on a value produced several times a tick. |
| `UserInputType` | `Enum.UserInputType` | — | read-only | What kind of input this is. The coarse question, for a handler that does not care which key. |

## Random

A seeded pseudorandom generator, and the only sanctioned source of randomness in simulation code (R10). A seeded stream is reproducible: the same seed yields the same sequence for the same engine build on the same platform, which is the level-B guarantee recorded replays rest on -- replays store seeds, not draws (ADR 0025).

## Random — constructors

### `new(seed: number? = nil): Random`

A generator seeded with `seed`, truncated toward zero. **Omitting the seed draws one from the host and is not legal in simulation code**: it is exactly the unseeded RNG R10 forbids, and `luaug check` flags it. Use it for cosmetics that never reach the world hash, or seed it from something the simulation already knows.

## Random — methods

### `Clone(): Random`

A copy positioned at the same point in the stream, continuing the same sequence independently of the original. This is how a subsystem takes a deterministic branch without consuming draws the rest of the frame is counting on.

### `NextInteger(min: number, max: number): number`

The next integer in [min, max], inclusive at **both** ends. This is the one place the engine is not half-open, which is why it is spelled out rather than inferred from `NextNumber`. `min > max`, or a non-integer bound, raises `script.err.random_range`.

### `NextNumber(min: number? = 0, max: number? = 1): number`

The next number in [min, max), defaulting to [0, 1) -- half-open, like every other range in the engine. `min > max` raises `script.err.random_range`.

### `NextUnitVector(): vector`

A direction drawn **uniformly over the sphere**, not merely one of unit length -- normalizing three independent draws clusters at the cube's corners, and this does not.

## RaycastParams

What a cast is allowed to hit. Every query on `Workspace` takes one, and omitting it means everything queryable. Constructed from a table so that a call site reads as the question it is asking rather than as four positional arguments (§2.3).

## RaycastParams — constructors

### `new(options: { Filter: { Instance }?, FilterType: Enum.RaycastFilterType?, CollisionGroup: string? }? = nil): RaycastParams`

Filter defaults to empty, FilterType to Exclude and CollisionGroup to the empty string, which means every group. An empty Exclude filter therefore hits everything, and an empty Include filter hits nothing -- which is what each word means and is worth knowing before a query silently returns nil.

## RaycastParams — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `CollisionGroup` | `string` | — | read-only | The group a hit must be in, or the empty string for any group. A camera ray asking for "Terrain" is cheaper than one that hits everything and filters afterwards. |
| `Filter` | `{ Instance }` | — | read-only | The instances the filter names, as a fresh array on every read. Descendants of a named instance are covered too, so filtering a Model filters its parts. |
| `FilterType` | `Enum.RaycastFilterType` | — | read-only | Whether Filter names what may be hit or what must be ignored. |

## RaycastResult

What a cast hit. Returned by `Workspace:Raycast` and `:Spherecast`, and nil when nothing was hit -- there is no "empty result" to check a field on, because a result that exists and means nothing is the shape of every nil-check somebody forgets.

## RaycastResult — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Distance` | `number` | — | read-only | How far along the cast the hit is, in metres. The direction passed to a cast is not normalised -- its length is the range -- so this is a distance rather than a fraction. |
| `Instance` | `BasePart` | — | read-only | The part that was hit. |
| `Normal` | `vector` | — | read-only | The surface normal there, pointing out of the surface. |
| `Position` | `vector` | — | read-only | Where on it, in world space. |

## Rect

A screen-space rectangle by two corners, in pixels. The corners are **not** sorted and not validated: an `ImageLabel.SliceCenter` whose min is past its max is a mistake for its author to see, not one for a constructor to silently correct.

A rectangle from its two corners.

| `Min` | `Vector2` | — | read-only | The corner given first. |
| `Width` | `number` | — | read-only | `Max.X - Min.X`, which is negative for an inverted rectangle rather than zero. |

## Signal

THE signal type, spelled `Signal<T...>` where the pack is what handlers receive and `Wait` returns -- never `RBXScriptSignal` (divergence #4). Delivery is **deferred only** (ADR 0015): a fire enqueues, and handlers run at the next drain in the order described in §3.1, with connection order guaranteed within one fire. Script-created signals replace BindableEvent and BindableFunction outright (divergence #5). Handler errors are contained: each runs on its own coroutine, and an error stops neither the other handlers, nor the drain, nor the firing script.

## Signal — constructors

### `new(): Signal<T...>`

A script-owned signal. The pack is generic and inferred from the `Fire` and `Connect` sites; annotate it (`Signal<string>`, `Signal<()>`) where inference has nothing to work from, such as an array element type.

## Signal — methods

### `Connect(handler: (T...) -> ()): Connection`

Registers `handler` and returns the Connection that ends it. Handlers of one fire run in the order they were connected; ordering *between* different signals is queue order and relying on it is a bug. `ConnectParallel` is a reserved name, absent in v1.

### `Destroy()`

Closes the signal. Already-queued fires find no live connections and invoke nothing, and every Connection reports `Connected == false` once the drain ends. Only script-created signals are destroyable; an instance's own signals are closed by `Instance:Destroy`.

### `Fire(values: T...)`

Enqueues an invocation of every current handler. Nothing runs before the next drain. Arguments are captured by reference and not copied: mutating a table between the fire and the drain is visible to the handlers.

### `Once(handler: (T...) -> ()): Connection`

Registers `handler` for a single invocation, disconnecting as it is invoked -- so a signal fired twice before a drain still calls it exactly once. A handler that errors has still been consumed.

### `Wait(): T...`

**Yields.** The calling thread parks until it completes.

Parks the calling coroutine as a one-shot registration made at the moment of the call, resumed by the next fire it is eligible for and returning that fire's arguments. It takes its place among the connections by registration order, so a Wait registered between handlers A and B resumes between them.

## Tween

A running property animation, returned by `TweenService:Create`. A value type rather than an Instance, like `AnimationTrack` (§2.2): nothing parents a tween, nothing finds one in the tree, and a class in the hierarchy that no tree ever holds would be a class every tree walk has to know is not there.

A tween writes through the SAME property setter a script writes through, so a tweened value fires `GetPropertyChangedSignal`, is filtered when it does not change, and is refused when it is out of range -- exactly as an assignment is. It steps on the sim tick, which is what makes it reproducible.

It keeps its target alive only as a reference: a tween on a destroyed instance stops and reports `Cancelled` rather than raising.

## Tween — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Completed` | `Signal<EnumPlaybackState>` | — | read-only | Fires once, carrying the state that ended the tween -- `Completed` for one that reached its end, `Cancelled` for one that was stopped. It is a PROPERTY here rather than an event because a `Tween` is a value type and only classes declare events; the signal it holds behaves like any other. The distinction between the two end states matters more than it looks: code that awards a checkpoint on a finished animation must not award it on an interrupted one. |
| `Instance` | `Instance?` | — | read-only | What this tween is animating, or nil once that instance has been destroyed. |
| `PlaybackState` | `Enum.PlaybackState` | — | read-only | Where it is in its life. |
| `TweenInfo` | `TweenInfo` | — | read-only | The timing it was created with. |

## Tween — methods

### `Cancel()`

Ends it before its time. The property keeps whatever value it had reached: cancelling is not undoing, and a tween that snapped back would be impossible to interrupt gracefully. `Completed` fires with `Cancelled`.

### `Pause()`

Stops it where it is, leaving the property at its current value. `Play` resumes.

### `Play()`

Starts it, or resumes a paused one from where it stopped. Playing a tween that is already playing is a no-op rather than a restart -- restarting is what a fresh `Create` is for, and a `Play` that silently rewound would make a hover effect stutter every frame the pointer moved.

## TweenInfo

How a tween moves: how long, along what curve, how many times, and after what delay (§2.3). Immutable, like every value type here -- a `TweenInfo` handed to two tweens cannot be changed under one of them.

The time is in SimClock seconds, the same seconds `task.wait` counts, so a tween is a whole number of ticks and a replay reproduces it exactly (ADR 0039's sibling argument: a system whose whole purpose is writing properties must not read the wall clock to decide what to write).

## TweenInfo — constructors

### `new(time: number? = 1, easingStyle: Enum.EasingStyle? = Enum.EasingStyle.Quad, easingDirection: Enum.EasingDirection? = Enum.EasingDirection.Out, repeatCount: number? = 0, reverses: boolean? = false, delayTime: number? = 0): TweenInfo`

The defaults are a one-second Quad-Out with no repeat, no reverse and no delay, which is the tween most UI wants. A negative `time` or `delayTime` raises; a negative `repeatCount` means repeat forever, which is the one negative number here that means something.

## TweenInfo — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `DelayTime` | `number` | — | read-only | Seconds before the first traversal begins, and before each repeat. Nothing is written during a delay -- the property keeps whatever it had. |
| `EasingDirection` | `Enum.EasingDirection` | — | read-only | Which end the curve eases. |
| `EasingStyle` | `Enum.EasingStyle` | — | read-only | The curve. |
| `RepeatCount` | `number` | — | read-only | How many EXTRA traversals follow the first. 0 plays once; 2 plays three times; a negative number repeats until something cancels it. |
| `Reverses` | `boolean` | — | read-only | Whether each traversal is followed by the same traversal backwards. A reversing tween takes twice `Time` per repeat and ends where it started. |
| `Time` | `number` | — | read-only | Seconds for ONE traversal, not counting delay, repeats or the return half of a reverse. |

## TweenInfo — operators

| Operator | Signature | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `__eq` | `(other: TweenInfo): boolean` | Exact, field by field. |

## UDim

One axis of a UI coordinate: a fraction of the parent (`Scale`) plus a pixel offset (`Offset`). The pair is what lets a layout written once be correct at every resolution -- "half the parent, minus eight pixels" is one value rather than a formula every caller re-derives when the window resizes. Adds and subtracts component-wise.

## UDim — constructors

### `new(scale: number? = 0, offset: number? = 0): UDim`

A UDim from a scale and an offset, both defaulting to 0.

## UDim — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Offset` | `number` | — | read-only | The pixel offset added after the scale is resolved. |
| `Scale` | `number` | — | read-only | The fraction of the parent's size along this axis. 1 is the whole parent; it is not clamped, so a value past 1 or below 0 is legal and means what it says. |

## UDim — operators

| Operator | Signature | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `__add` | `(other: UDim): UDim` | Adds both halves. |
| `__sub` | `(other: UDim): UDim` | Subtracts both halves. |
| `__eq` | `(other: UDim): boolean` | Exact equality of both halves. |

## UDim2

A two-axis UI coordinate: a `UDim` per axis. Every `Position` and `Size` on a UIObject is one, which is what makes a layout written once correct at every resolution.

## UDim2 — constructors

### `fromOffset(xo: number? = 0, yo: number? = 0): UDim2`

Pixels on both axes, zero scales -- the spelling for a fixed-size element.

### `fromScale(xs: number? = 0, ys: number? = 0): UDim2`

Scale on both axes, zero offsets -- the spelling for a purely relative layout.

### `new(xs: number? = 0, xo: number? = 0, ys: number? = 0, yo: number? = 0): UDim2`

Four numbers in axis order: x scale, x offset, y scale, y offset. There is deliberately no second overload taking two UDims -- one constructor with one argument order is what a frozen surface is for.

## UDim2 — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `X` | `UDim` | — | read-only | The horizontal axis. |
| `Y` | `UDim` | — | read-only | The vertical axis. |

## UDim2 — methods

### `Lerp(goal: UDim2, alpha: number): UDim2`

Interpolates all four numbers independently. This is the operation a tween on a `Position` performs, and it is on the type so that game code animating by hand and the engine animating by tween produce the same intermediate values.

## UDim2 — operators

| Operator | Signature | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `__add` | `(other: UDim2): UDim2` | Adds both axes. |
| `__sub` | `(other: UDim2): UDim2` | Subtracts both axes. |
| `__eq` | `(other: UDim2): boolean` | Exact equality of all four numbers. |

## Vector2

A two-component screen-space vector, in f32. Userdata rather than a primitive, because the native Luau `vector` is three-wide and IS Vector3 (ADR 0013) -- which is why this is the one vector type in the surface whose operators are the engine's rather than the language's. It carries the arithmetic UI code actually writes: `+`, `-`, unary `-`, `*` and `/` with a scalar on either side or component-wise with another Vector2, and an exact `==`.

## Vector2 — constants

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `one` | `Vector2` | — | read-only | `Vector2.new(1, 1)`, as a constant rather than a call. |
| `zero` | `Vector2` | — | read-only | `Vector2.new(0, 0)`, as a constant rather than a call. |

## Vector2 — constructors

### `new(x: number? = 0, y: number? = 0): Vector2`

A vector from two components, each defaulting to 0.

## Vector2 — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Magnitude` | `number` | — | read-only | The vector's length. |
| `Unit` | `Vector2` | — | read-only | The same direction at length 1. The zero vector normalizes to zero rather than to NaN, which matches Vector3 and is what stops a stationary input axis poisoning a frame. |
| `X` | `number` | — | read-only | The horizontal component. Uppercase, unlike `Vector3.x`: that one is lowercase because it is a field of the Luau primitive itself (divergence #9), and this type is ours. |
| `Y` | `number` | — | read-only | The vertical component, growing downward in every screen-space coordinate the UI uses. |

## Vector2 — methods

### `Dot(other: Vector2): number`

The dot product with another vector.

### `Lerp(goal: Vector2, alpha: number): Vector2`

Linear interpolation toward `goal`. `alpha` is not clamped, so a value outside 0-1 extrapolates.

## Vector2 — operators

| Operator | Signature | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `__add` | `(other: Vector2): Vector2` | Component-wise addition. |
| `__sub` | `(other: Vector2): Vector2` | Component-wise subtraction. |
| `__unm` | `(): Vector2` | Negation. |
| `__mul` | `(other: Vector2): Vector2` | Component-wise multiplication. |
| `__mul` | `(scalar: number): Vector2` | Scaling. The scalar may be on either side, because `__mul` dispatches on either operand. |
| `__div` | `(other: Vector2): Vector2` | Component-wise division. |
| `__div` | `(scalar: number): Vector2` | Division by a scalar, on either side. |
| `__eq` | `(other: Vector2): boolean` | Exact, component-wise equality -- an identity test rather than a tolerance. |

## Vector3

The 3-component f32 vector, which IS the Luau VM's native `vector` primitive rather than a userdata wrapping one (ADR 0013): `typeof` answers `"vector"`, arithmetic allocates nothing, and the components are the primitive's own lowercase `x`/`y`/`z` -- the single documented exception to the casing rules (§9). The `Vector3` global is the `vector` library plus `new`, so every function below is reachable under both names and `Vector3.zero == vector.zero`; it is a superset table and no table identity is promised. Operators are the primitive's own and all of them: `+`, `-` (binary and unary), `*` and `/` with a scalar on either side or component-wise with another vector, `//`, `%`, and `==`. Precision is millimetre-exact to roughly ±8 km and degrades to ~16 mm at ±131 km where the exponent range ends, which is why open-world math goes through CFrame's f64 translation and not through a position (ADR 0013 addendum, ADR 0014).

## Vector3 — constants

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `one` | `vector` | — | read-only | `(1, 1, 1)`, the identity for component-wise multiplication. |
| `zero` | `vector` | — | read-only | `(0, 0, 0)`. Reachable as both `vector.zero` and `Vector3.zero`, and equal either way. |

## Vector3 — constructors

### `abs(v: vector): vector`

Each component's absolute value.

### `angle(a: vector, b: vector, axis: vector? = nil): number`

The angle between two vectors in radians, in [0, π]. With `axis`, the result is signed about it by the right-hand rule and so spans (-π, π] -- which is the only way to tell a rotation from its mirror image.

### `ceil(v: vector): vector`

Each component rounded toward positive infinity.

### `clamp(v: vector, min: vector, max: vector): vector`

Each component clamped into the box `min`..`max`. An inverted box is an error rather than an empty result, because there is no component value that satisfies it.

### `create(x: number, y: number, z: number? = 0): vector`

The official vector stdlib's spelling of the constructor, carried so that code written against another Luau runtime ports unchanged. Unlike `new` it requires `x` and `y`, because the stdlib checks argument count rather than accepting `nil` as zero.

### `cross(a: vector, b: vector): vector`

The cross product, right-handed like the world it describes: `cross(right, up) == -look` for any frame's basis (§2.3, handedness).

### `dot(a: vector, b: vector): number`

The dot product of two vectors.

### `floor(v: vector): vector`

Each component rounded toward negative infinity.

### `lerp(a: vector, b: vector, alpha: number): vector`

Component-wise linear interpolation from `a` to `b`. `alpha` is not clamped, so values outside [0, 1] extrapolate.

### `magnitude(v: vector): number`

The vector's length. Preferred over the `.Magnitude` field, which reaches the same number through the metatable and is measurably slower.

### `max(a: vector, rest: ...vector): vector`

The component-wise maximum of every argument -- the opposite corner of the bounding box `min` returns.

### `min(a: vector, rest: ...vector): vector`

The component-wise minimum of every argument -- a corner of the bounding box, not whichever argument is shortest.

### `new(x: number? = 0, y: number? = 0, z: number? = 0): vector`

Constructs a vector; a missing component is 0. Bound as the `vectorCtor` compile option so a literal call is constant-folded and a dynamic one is a fastcall -- neither allocates.

### `normalize(v: vector): vector`

The vector scaled to unit length. A zero vector has no direction to preserve and normalizing one yields NaN components rather than an error.

### `sign(v: vector): vector`

Each component reduced to -1, 0 or 1 by its sign.

## Vector3 — properties

| Name | Type | Default | Access | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `Magnitude` | `number` | — | read-only | The vector's length, reached through the primitive's metatable. It is a convenience for readability at the cost of speed: `vector.magnitude(v)` is a fastcall and this is not. |
| `Unit` | `vector` | — | read-only | The vector scaled to length 1, reached through the metatable. Prefer `vector.normalize(v)` in hot code for the same reason as `Magnitude`. |
| `x` | `number` | — | read-only | The X component. Lowercase because it is a field of the VM primitive itself, like a string's length, and not a member of a type this project defines -- the one documented exception to the PascalCase rule (§9, divergence #9). `v.X` reads the same component rather than raising, because the interpreter answers a single-character index on a vector case-insensitively before any metatable is consulted; lowercase is still the only spelling declared, so the uppercase one is a type error. |
| `y` | `number` | — | read-only | The Y component, up in the engine's Y-up world. Lowercase for the same reason as `x`. |
| `z` | `number` | — | read-only | The Z component. Forward is -Z, so a forward-facing direction has a negative `z`. Lowercase for the same reason as `x`. |

## Vector3 — methods

### `Angle(other: vector, axis: vector? = nil): number`

The angle to `other` in radians; the method form of `vector.angle`, `axis` included, so the signed form is available without switching spelling.

### `Cross(other: vector): vector`

The cross product with `other`, in that order; the method form of `vector.cross`. The operation does not commute, so `a:Cross(b) == -b:Cross(a)`.

### `Dot(other: vector): number`

The dot product with `other`; the method form of `vector.dot`.

### `Lerp(goal: vector, alpha: number): vector`

Linear interpolation toward `goal`; the method form of `vector.lerp`. `alpha` is not clamped.
